Characteristics and intestinal immunomodulating activities of water-soluble pectic 
polysaccharides from Chenpi with different storage periods 
 
Running title: Characteristics and intestinal activities of pectic polysaccharides from Chenpi 
Changcheng Tian, a,* Hui Xu, a Jing Li, b Zhuo Han a 
 a Department of Food and Bioengineering, Bengbu College, Bengbu, Anhui, 233000, P .R. China 
 b Department of Life Sciences, Bengbu Medical College, Bengbu, Anhui, 233000, P .R. China 
Address for Correspondence 
Dr. Changcheng Tian 
Department of Food and Bioengineering, Bengbu College, Bengbu, Anhui, 233000, P .R. China 
E-mail: tianchangcheng2006@126.com 
 
 
Abstract 
BACKGROUND: Traditional view considers that the long-t erm stored Chenpi (dried citrus peel) 
has better health efficacies as compared with the fresh Chenpi, but the detailed mechanism 
remains obscure. 
RESULTS: The three water-soluble p ectic polysaccharides (CPP1, CPP5 and CPP10) were 
obtained from one-year, five-year and ten-year Chenpi, respectively, and their physicochemical 
characteristics and intestinal immunomodulating activities were investigated and compared. Our 
results showed that CPP5 and CPP10 showed the lower dynamic viscosity and degree of 
methylesterification, as well as the higher mol ecular heterogeneity as compared with CPP1. The 
monosaccharide composition analysis indicated that CPP1 was composed of arabinose,

galacturonic acid, galactose and a little of rhamnose, however CPP5 and CPP10 consisted of 
arabinose, galacturonic acid, galactose, glucose, xylose and a little of rhamnose . With the 
extension of storage period of Chenpi, the content of soluble conjugate phenolic acids increased in 
the pectic polysaccharide. Furthermore, it was pr oven that the pectic polysaccharides extracted 
from the five-year and ten-year Chenpi could significantly enhance the proliferation of bone 
marrow cells via activating the Peyer’s patch cells in vitro. 
CONCLUSION: The present study demonstrat ed the differences of the pectic polysaccharides 
from Chenpi with different storage periods, and proved that the pectic polysaccharides extracted 
from the long-term stored Chenpi had the more sign ificant intestinal activities than that from the 
fresh Chenpi. This phenomenon might partly explain why the long-term stored Chenpi had better 
health care effects.

INTRODUCTION 
Citrus peel is regarded as a by-product in the process of juice manufacture, but actually it contains 
a variety of bioactive compounds, such as phenolic acids,
1 flavonoids, 2 limonoids 3 and 
coumarins,4 which is an exploitable biological resour ce. Dried citrus peel, known as Chenpi, has 
been used as a Chinese herbal medicine and functional beverage for promoting digestion of 
gastrointestinal tract in China and other Asian coun tries for centuries. Moreover, citrus peel is one 
of the main raw materials for pectin production. 
Pectin is a type of complex heteropolysaccharide that abundantly exists in the primary cell wall of 
dicot and non-graminaceous species, and its structure is too complicated to be clarified 
completely so far. It was proved that the pectin existing in citrus peels contained a backbone chain

Accepted Article
 
that was composed of partly methyl-esterified α-D-galacturonic acids, which was substituted with 
various branch chains, such as rhamnogalacturonan I (RG- I) and rhamnogalacturonan II 
(RG-II).5 Recent researches reported that some pectic fragments obtained by enzymatic 
degradation exhibited the significant biological activities, such as prebiotic property,6 antitumor 
metastasis7 and antidiabetic.8 Especially, the intestinal immunomodulating actions of pectic 
fragments attracted the more and more interests and attentions of researchers.9,10 Suh et al. 
demonstrated that a pectic polysaccharide (CUI-3 II b-3-2) purified from the peel of Citrus unshiu 
could stimulate the Peyer’s patch cells to produce interleukin-6, and further enhanced the 
proliferation of bone marrow cells, suggesting the potent intestinal immune activity.11 
Traditional Chinese medicine considers that the long er the storage period of Chenpi, the better its 
efficacy. This phenomenon has usually been attributed to the change of active small 
molecules in aged Chenpi, such as phenolic acids and flavonoids. Choi et al. demonstrated that 
the three-year Chenpi extract possessed the higher total phen olic content and the superior 
radical-scavenging activity as compared with the one-year Chenpi extract. 12 Guo et al. also 
reported that the aged Chenpi contained the more 5-demethylated polymethoxyflavones 
(5-OH PMFs) that likely affected the anti-lipogenic activity of Chenpi extract. 13 However, the 
research focus on pectin had been still limited. In this study, the three water-soluble pectic 
polysaccharides (CPP1, CPP5 and CPP10) were extracte d from one-year, five-year and ten-year 
Chenpi (Citrus reticulata cv. Chachiensis), respectively, by the method of hot water extraction and 
alcohol precipitation. The physicochemical ch aracteristics of pectic polysaccharides were 
preliminarily investigated and compared, and their intestinal immunomodulating activities against 
the Peyer’s patch cells were evaluated.

MATERIALS AND METHODS 
Materials and reagents 
One-year, five-year and ten-year peels of C. reticulata were purchased from Xinhui region of 
Guangdong province, China. So far, the production of Xinhui Chenpi has still followed the 
traditional technology. In brief, the fresh citrus peel is dried in the sun and then stored in a 
ventilated and dry situation for maturing. 
Standard dextrans (5.0, 25.0, 80.0, 150.0, 470.0 and 610.0 KDa), monosaccharide (D-glucose, 
D-galactose, L-rhamnose, L-arab inose, D-xylose, galacturonic acid) and apple pectin were 
purchased from Sigma Chemical Co. (St. Louis, MO, USA). DEAE-cellulose D-52 was 
purchased from Beijing Solarbio Science & technology co., ltd (Beijing, China). 
Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and 1-pheny-3-methyl-5-pyrazolone (PMP) were purchased from 
Sinopharm Chemical Reageni Co., Ltd. RPMI 1640 medium and fetal bovine serum (FBS) were 
purchased from Gibco BRL Co. (Grand Island, NY, USA). Male mouse (Kunming) were provided 
by Bengbu Medical College. All other reagents were analytical grade or chromatographic grade. 
Sample extraction 
The dried Chenpi (50.0 g) were chopped into small pieces and dipped into 1.0 L of 95% ethanol 
for 24 h to remove the pigments and lipids. After dried, the peels were extracted with 1.0 L of 
distilled water at 95 ℃ for 2 h with constant stirring. The extract was filtered, centrifuged at 4500 
g for 10.0 min, and then concentrated to 1/3 of its initial volume using a vacuum rotary 
evaporation apparatus. The filtrate was precipitated by adding ethanol to a final concentration of 
80% (v/v) for 24 h at 4 ℃. The resulted precipitate was dissolved in suitable amount of distilled 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

Accepted Article
 
water and deproteinized by the Sevag method 14 for five times. After that, the sample was dialyzed 
against distilled water for 24 h and lyophilized. The three samples were named as CPP1, CPP5 
and CPP10, respectively, according to the storage periods. 
General methods 
The total carbohydrate content and protein content were determined by the phenol-sulfuric 
method15 and the Bradford method, 16 respectively. The uronic acid content was measured by the 
m-hydroxybiphenyl method. 17 The dynamic viscosity of each sample (10 g L -1, dissolved in 
distilled water) was measured using a rheometer (Brookfield, Rheo 3000) at the shear rate of 150 
rpm.The relative molecular weight was investigated using a high performance liquid 
chromatographic system (Agilent 1260, USA) equipped with the two serial columns 
(TSKG4000PWXL and TSKG5000PWXL). The elution was kept at 0.5 mL min -1 using 10 mmol 
L-1 N a C l s o l u t i o n a s e l u e n t . Six standard dextrans were analyzed in the same conditions to 
give a calibrated curve. The relative mole cular weight of each sample was estimated 
according to the calibrated curve. 
Each of the samples was further fractionated by the anion exchange chromatography 
(DEAE-cellulose 52, 3.5×15 cm ) eluted with distilled water , 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 mol L -1 NaCl 
solutions successively. The elution rate was 5 mL min-1, and each eluent was collected for 20 tubes 
(10 mL tube -1) by a fraction collector. The total sugar co ntent in each tube was measured by the 
phenol-H2SO4 method. 
Infrared spectrum 
After dried at 50 ℃ for 12 h, the pectic sample was pressed into pellet with KBr powder and 
scanned using a Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometer (N icolet 67, Thermo Nicolet) in

Accepted Article
 
the range of 4000-400 cm-1. 
Monosaccharide composition 
The monosaccharide composition of pectic sample was determined using the pre-colunm 
derivatization high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) 18 method with some 
modifications. Each of the samples (2.0 mg) was dissolved in 2.0 mL of trifluoroacetic acid (2.0 
mol L -1) and sealed in an ampoule bottle. The hydrolysis reaction lasted for 6 h at 110 ℃.The 
resulted hydrolysate was evaporated to dryness and dissolved in 1.0 mL of distilled water, and 
then 50 μL of the hydrolysate was mixed with 150 μL of 0.3 mol L-1 NaOH solution and 100 μL of 
0.5 mol L-1 PMP (dissolved with methanol) successively. The mixture was neutralized with 150 μL 
HCl (0.3 mol L-1) following reacting for 30 min at 70 ℃. The reaction solution was extracted with 
chloroform for three times and the aqueous layer was used for HPLC analysis. All the 
monosaccharide standards were treated with the same method. A HPLC system (Waters 2487, 
USA) equipped with a C18 analytical column (Shim-Pack VP-ODS, 150×4.6, 3102772, USA) was 
used for the monosaccharide analysis. The mobile phase A was acetonitrile-0.05 mol L -1 KH2PO4 
(15:85, v/v), an d B was acetonitrile-0.05 mol L -1 KH 2PO4 (40:60, v/v). The gradient elution of 
18-25-100-100% B by a linear increase from 0 to 25 to 27 to 30 min was executed. The flow rate 
of elution was kept at 1.0 mL min-1, and UV absorbance of the effluent was 250 nm. The retention 
time and peak area were used for the qualitative and quantitative analysis, respectively. 
Extraction of phenolic compounds 
The phenolic compounds in each sample were extracted according to the previous method 19 with 
the slight modification. Briefly, the pectic sample (1.0 g) was extracted with 20 mL of 70% 
methanol/70% acetone (1:1, v/v) mixture thrice to give residue A and supernatant A. After 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

Accepted Article
 
concentrated under reduced pressure, the supernatant A was acidified to pH 2.0 with 6 mol L-1 HCl, 
and extracted with equal-volume hexane and diet hyl ether/ethyl acetate mixture (DE/EA, 1:1, v/v) 
successively. The resulted organic layer was dehydrat ed with sodium sulfate, and then dried at 40 ℃ 
to give the free phenolic acids. The remaining aqueous phase was evaporated to dryness and 
hydrolyzed by NaOH solution (4.0 mol L -1) for 4.0 h. After acidified to pH 2.0, the sample was 
extracted with hexane and DE/EA (1:1, v/v) succes sively to give the soluble conjugate phenolic 
acids. The insoluble-bound phenolic acids were extracted from the residue A according to the 
process described for the separation of soluble conjugate phenolic acids. 
Determination of total phenolic content 
The total phenolic content was measured by the Folin-Ciocalteau method as described in the 
previous work. 20 Briefly, 0.5 mL of the phenolic extract solution (1.0 mg mL -1, dissolved with 
methanol) was mixed with 0.5 mL of Folin-Ciocalteau’s phenol reagent in a tube, and then 1.0 mL 
of Na2CO3 solution (75 g L -1) and 8.0 mL of distilled water were successively added to the tube. 
The mixture solution reacted for 45 min at ambien t temperature, and the ab sorbance was read at 
725 nm. Gallic acid was used as the standard subs tance to prepare the regression curve, and the 
total phenolic content of each sample was expre ssed as mg of gallic acid equivalents (GAE) per 
gram of pectin. 
Intestinal immunomodulating activity of Chenpi pectin in vitro 
The intestinal immunomodulating activity of pe ctic sample was evaluated according to the 
previous procedure.21 In brief, 180 μL of Peyer’s patch cells suspension (2.5 × 10 6 cells mL -1 in 
RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% FBS) was cultured with distilled H 2O (control group, 
20 μL), apple pectin (negative group, 20 μL) and pectic samples (test groups, 20 μL), respectively,

Accepted Article
 
in a 96-well plate for 5 d at 37 ℃ in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO 2-95% air. The resulting 
culture supernatant (50 μL) was further cultured with the bone marrow cell suspension (5 × 10 5 
cells mL-1 in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 10% FBS, 100 μL) in a humidified atmosphere of 5% 
CO2-95% air at 37 ℃ for 6 d. In addition, each of the pect ins was directly added into the bone 
marrow cell suspension, and the mixture was incubated according to the conditions above. 
The proliferation of bone marrow cells was measured by Alamar BlueTM reduction method. Briefly, 
20 μL of Alamar Blue was added into each well of bone marrow cell cultures, and continued to 
incubate for 6 h. The resulting cultures were measured using a fluorospectro photometer (F-4500, 
Hitachi, Japan) at an excitation wavelength of 544 nm and an emission wavelength of 590 nm. 
E a c h e x p e r i m e n t w a s r e p e a t e d f o r t h r e e t i m e s . 
Data analysis 
All values were expressed as mean ± SD 。Statistical significance was determined using Student’s 
t-test. A value of p < 0.05 indicated the statistical significance. 
 
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 
Preparation and characteristics of Chenpi pectins 
Chenpi has usually been used as a functional hot drink in China and other Asian countries, so the 
water-soluble pectic polysaccharides were the research focus. In this study, the three water-soluble 
extracts (CPP1, CPP5 and CPP10) were obtained from one-year, five-year and ten-year Chenpi, 
respectively, by the method of hot water extraction and alcohol precipitation. All the extracts were 
rich in carbohydrate and contained a certain amount of uronic acids, suggesting their pectic 
potential. As shown in Table 1, the yields of pectic extracts from five-year and ten-year Chenpi 
This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

Accepted Article
 
were significantly higher than that from one-yea r Chenpi. Moreover, the viscosities of pectic 
extracts (1 mg mL -1, dissolved in distilled water) lowered with the extension of storage period of 
Chenpi. These suggested the solubility of pectic polysaccharides in Chenpi increased with the 
extension of storage period. The change of pectic solubility migh t be related to its molecular 
structure, such as the molecular weight and degree of methylesterification (DM).22 
In order to testify our assumption above, the relative molecular weight of the samples were 
investigated by high performance size exclusion chromatography (HPSEC) as shown in Fig.1. The 
three samples presented a similar main peak, and the retention time in the columns was about 21 
minutes. The relative molecular weights of CPP1, CPP5 and CPP10 were 4.18 ×105, 3.73×
105 and 4.02 ×105 Da, respectively, according to the standard curve of the dextrans. In 
comparison, the peak of CPP10 was broader, which suggested the depolymerisation of pectin. The 
FTIR spectrums of the three samples displayed the typical absorption peaks of carbohydrate, 
including the stretching vibration of O-H (3417 cm -1) and C-C (1108 cm -1) as illustrated in Fig.2. 
The peaks at 1743 cm -1 and 1630 cm -1 were attributed to the vibrations of esterified carboxylic 
group and free carboxylic group, respectively. 23 In this study, the DM of pectin was estimated 
based on the ratio of the peak area at 1743 cm -1 to sum of the peak areas at 1743 cm -1 and 1630 
cm-1 in FT-IR spectra.24 Hereby, the DMs of CPP1, CPP5 and CPP10 were 39.26%, 28.33%, and 
26.53%, respectively. It was obvious that all the pectic samples belonged to the low 
methylesterification pectin (DM < 50%), and th e DMs decreased with the extension of storage 
period. 
The monosaccharide composition analysis wa s executed by the high performance liquid 
chromatography, which was helpful for investigation of uronic acids. The results showed that

CPP1 was mainly composed of arabinose, galact ose and galacturonic acid. In comparison, CPP5 
and CPP10 also contained the glucose and xylo se besides the monosaccharide types in CPP1. 
Moreover, the content of galacturonic acid in CPP5 and CPP10 significantly decreased, but the 
content of arabinose increased as shown in Table 1. 
Each of the samples was further fractionated by the DEAE-cellulose ani on exchange resin as 
illustrated in Fig.3. CPP1 presented two peaks as eluted with the distilled water and 0.2 mol L -1 
NaCl solution. CPP5 presented five peaks as eluted by distilled water, 0.05, 0.1 and 0.2 mol 
L-1 NaCl solution. CPP10 showed the more peaks when eluted by distilled water, 0.1, 0.2 and 
0.3 mol L -1 NaCl solution. As we all known, the separation of ion exchange resin is mainly 
depended on the charge strength of molecule, and the elution peak corresponding to 
high-concentration salt solution indicates a strong binding force between adsorbates and ion 
exchange resin. Thus, it could be inferred that the heterogeneity of pectic polysaccharides 
increased with the extension of storage period of Chenpi. 
Separation and measurement of phenolic compounds in Chenpi pectin 
It has been proven that most of natural pectins are ester-linked to phenolic compounds in various 
ways.25 In this study, the free, solu ble conjugate and insoluble-bound phenolic acids in the pectic 
samples were extracted and measured, respectively (Table 2). The contents of free phenolic acids 
in all the samples were low possibly due to the previous ethanol precipitation and deproteinization. 
The contents of soluble conjugate phenolic acids in CPP1, CPP5 and CPP10 were 43.0 ± 0.4, 62.0 
± 0.3 and 65.0 ± 0.3 mg g -1, respectively. It was found that th e pectic samples extracted from the 
long-term stored Chenpi contained the more soluble phenolic acids. 
Intestinal immunomodulating activity of Chenpi pectin

Peyer’s patches are parts of gut-associated lympho reticular tissues (GALT) and play an essential 
role in uptake of antigen and initia tion of intestinal immune response. 26 Some exogenous 
substances, known as immunomodulators, can activate the plasmablasts and regulatory T 
lymphocytes that exist in the Peyer’s patches, and enhance the defense system of body. 27 Some 
natural immunomodulators are regarded as potential ingredients for body health. As shown in Fig. 
4, CPP5 and CPP10 displayed the significant stimulating effects as compared to the control group, 
however CPP1 showed the effective effe ct just at the concentration of 50 μg mL. Meanwhile, our 
work also proved that these pectic samples could not directly induce the proliferation of bone 
marrow cells (data not shown), which was in agreement with the previous research.11 
Natural pectin contains a variety of t ypical structural moieties, such as RG- I and RG- II. The 
backbone of RG-I is composed of repeating disaccharide [ →4)-α-D-GalpA-(1→2)- 
α-L-Rhap(1→], in which the C(O)-4 and/or C(O)-3 positions of α-L-Rhap were partially 
substituted with a variety of side -chains, such as arabinogalactan- I (AG-I), arabinogalactan- II 
(AG-II) and arabinan. 28 AG- I is an arabinosyl-substituted derivative of linear 1,4-linked 
β-D-galactosyl residues, an d the most abundant RG- I associated structural regions in some 
pectins.9 AG-II usually occurs in the proteoglycans known as arabinogalactan-proteins (AGP) or 
covalently linked to RG- I backbone.29 In addition to arabinose and galactose, AG- II also contains 
other neutral sugars.30 In this study, the three water-solu ble polysaccharides mainly consisted 
of arabinose, galacturonic acid and galactos e, which possibly suggested the existence of 
arabinogalactan (AG) and arabinan. As compared with CPP1, CPP5 and CPP10 contained 
the more arabinose and the le ss galacturonic acid. Meanwhile, the more monosaccharide 
types were found in CPP5 and CPP10. Thus, it could be inferred that the pectic polysaccharides

in Chenpi executed a sequential degradation actio n with the extension of storage period, which 
partly explained why long-term stored Chenpi had the better health care effects. 
Moreover, most pectins link with phenolic acids via ester bond, so they are often referred as 
“feruloylated pectins”. 31 Our results showed that the wate r-soluble pectic polysaccharides 
extracted from the long-term stor ed Chenpi (five years above) contained the more soluble 
conjugate phenolic acids than that from the fres h Chenpi. The increase of soluble phenolic ester 
seemed to exert a positive influence on the pectic activities in Chenpi, however further 
investigation was needed. 
 
CONCLUSION 
The present study investigated and compared the physicochemical characteristics and intestinal 
immunomodulating activities of the three water-so luble pectic polysaccharides from the different 
aged Chenpi. The pectic polysaccharides from the long-term stored Chenpi (five-year and ten-year) 
displayed the lower DM, the higher molecula r heterogeneity and the more complicated 
monosaccharide components, as compared with that from the fresh Chenpi (one-year). Meanwhile, 
it was found that the pectic samp les from the long-term stored Chenpi contained the more soluble 
conjugate phenolic acids. All the pe ctic polysccharides were proved to exert a positive effect on 
the the Peyer’s patches cells in vitro, but the pectic samples from the long-term stored Chenpi 
were more effective. Based on th e results above, it could be conc luded that the activities of the 
long-term stored Chenpi possibly had a relationship with the pectic derivatives in Chenpi. This 
work presented a new viewpoint to understand why long-term stored Chenpi had better functional 
activities, and the analysis of pectic characteristic might be used as a novel method to evaluate the
